subcategory: East Asian dioecious ornamental fruiting shade tree

planting.note: Plant container-grown nursery stock in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; because the species is dioecious, place at least one male tree near female trees to ensure fruit set, and allow ample room since mature specimens form a broad, rounded canopy.

directions: Idesia polycarpa is a fast-growing deciduous tree native to the forests of China, Japan, and Korea, grown chiefly for its bold, heart-shaped leaves on long red petioles and its dramatic autumn display of hanging fruit clusters. Female trees produce pendant strands of small round berries that ripen from green to orange-red in fall and persist into winter, drawing flocks of robins, waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds once other food sources have dwindled. In late spring the tree bears small, fragrant, greenish-yellow flowers in drooping panicles, with male flowers slightly showier than the female ones that follow them into fruit. Site it in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with room to develop its broad canopy, and expect a largely trouble-free, fast-growing specimen tree once established.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Direct sow seed or set out divisions and container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy, salt-tolerant soil in full sun; this subtropical shrub grows naturally along rocky and sandy shorelines of the Florida Keys and Caribbean, where it tolerates salt spray, brackish sand, and periodic tidal flooding.

directions: Green sea oxeye is a woody-based, shrubby perennial of Florida Keys and West Indian shorelines, forming a rounded mound of succulent, glossy, deep-green leaves that distinguish it from its more silvery-leaved mainland relative, sea oxeye daisy (Borrichia frutescens). Bright yellow button-centered daisy flowers appear nearly year-round in its native subtropical range, drawing butterflies and small native bees to coastal gardens where few other flowering shrubs tolerate the salt-laden air. It thrives in lean, fast-draining sandy or rocky soil and needs no irrigation once rooted, making it a dependable, low-maintenance choice for beachfront and xeric coastal landscaping in the warmest parts of zone 10 and all of zone 11. Because it is frost-tender, gardeners outside its tropical range should treat it as a container or protected-bed specimen rather than a hardy landscape shrub.
sources: Institute for Regional Conservation – Natives For Your Neighborhood

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with afternoon shade; provide a trellis, arbor, or fence, since this twining vine reaches 15-25 ft and tolerates more summer heat than its northern relative Schisandra chinensis.

directions: Native to the warm-temperate woodlands of central China, southern schisandra is a deciduous twining vine closely related to the better-known Schisandra chinensis, but better adapted to hot, humid summer climates such as the Gulf Coast. Dioecious like its relative, it needs a male and female vine growing nearby for the females to set their drooping clusters of small, tart, red berries in late summer and fall. Small, fragrant, pale pink to cream flowers open along the stems in spring before the foliage fully expands, followed by the ornamental fruit display that gives the plant its long history of use in traditional Chinese herbal preparations. Train it on a sturdy support in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade and consistently moist, well-drained soil, since it struggles in soil that dries out for extended periods.
sources: United States National Plant Germplasm System (GRIN-Global)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in bright light with some direct morning sun; grow primarily as a houseplant, patio plant, or bonsai subject, bringing it under cover well before the first frost.

directions: 'Flore Pleno' is a long-cultivated double-flowered selection of Serissa japonica, prized among bonsai enthusiasts for the dense rosettes of small white petals that replace the single, star-shaped blooms of the species. The tiny, glossy, boxwood-like leaves clothe a finely branched, twiggy habit that responds well to pruning and wiring, and the plant flushes with flowers almost continuously whenever light and temperature are favorable. Like other forms of Serissa, it resents being moved, over-watered, or allowed to dry out between waterings, and reacts to any of these stresses by dropping leaves and buds; steady conditions produce the most reliable bloom. Where winters are too cold for outdoor planting, keep it as a container specimen on a bright porch or windowsill and move it outdoors for summer once night temperatures stay above 50°F.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in spring or fall; like its better-known relative, shrub katsura needs consistent soil moisture, especially while young, and benefits from afternoon shade in hot inland climates.

directions: Cercidiphyllum magnificum is the smaller, shrubbier cousin of the familiar katsura tree, found in the mountain forests of central Honshu, Japan, where it typically grows as a multi-stemmed small tree or large shrub rather than the stately single-trunked form of Cercidiphyllum japonicum. Its rounded, heart-shaped leaves emerge with a soft reddish-bronze flush in spring, mature to blue-green through summer, and turn gold to apricot in fall, releasing the same caramel-like fragrance as the dropped leaves decompose. The exfoliating, orange-brown bark on older stems adds winter interest to a plant that remains far less common in cultivation than its larger relative. Grow it in a cool, moist, sheltered site with reliable summer moisture, since it is less tolerant of heat and drought than Cercidiphyllum japonicum and is best suited to cooler regions of its hardiness range.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Chinese maackia is adaptable to a range of soil types and, as a legume, fixes its own nitrogen and needs little supplemental fertilizer once established.

directions: Chinese maackia is a small to medium deciduous tree from central China, grown for its late-summer display of upright, creamy-white pea-flower racemes at a time when very few other trees are still blooming, and valued further for its lustrous, smooth, copper-colored bark that peels in papery curls on mature trunks. Compound leaves emerge with a silvery sheen in spring before settling into clean dark green through the growing season. Like its close relative Maackia amurensis, it is a legume that enriches the soil around its roots and tolerates urban stress, clay soil, and drought once established. It makes an excellent small specimen or street tree for gardeners wanting four-season interest and reliable flowering in a tree size that fits smaller landscapes.
sources: JC Raulston Arboretum at NC State University
